what_its_for: Fentanyl transdermal patches are used to treat moderate to severe long-lasting (chronic) pain in adults who need around-the-clock pain relief and are already tolerant to opioid pain medicines. It is a strong opioid (narcotic) pain medicine. It should NOT be used for pain that only comes and goes, or for pain right after surgery.
how_to_take: Apply the patch directly to your skin following these steps: (1) Choose a flat, hairless area of skin on your upper arm, chest, back, or the side of your chest. Avoid skin that is irritated, cut, burned, or oily. (2) If you need to remove hair from the area, clip it with scissors — do NOT shave it. (3) Clean the skin with plain water and let it dry completely before applying. Do NOT use soaps, lotions, or alcohol on the area. (4) Open the package and peel off the protective liner. Do NOT touch the sticky side. (5) Press the patch firmly onto your skin with the palm of your hand for about 30 seconds. Make sure all edges stick well. (6) Wash your hands right away with soap and water after applying. (7) Wear the patch continuously for 72 hours (3 days), then remove it and apply a new patch to a DIFFERENT skin site. Wait at least 3 days before using the same skin area again. (8) When removing an old patch, fold it in half with the sticky sides together and flush it down the toilet immediately. Never throw used patches in the trash where children or pets could find them.
dosing: Your doctor will prescribe the lowest dose that controls your pain. Patches come in different strengths (12, 25, 50, 75, and 100 micrograms per hour). Most people change their patch every 72 hours (3 days), but some people may need to change it every 48 hours — your doctor will tell you. Do NOT cut or damage the patch. Do NOT use more patches than prescribed. Heat can cause the patch to release medicine too fast — avoid heating pads, electric blankets, hot tubs, saunas, and long hot baths or showers while wearing the patch.
missed_dose: If you forget to change your patch at the scheduled time, apply a new patch as soon as you remember, then continue on your new schedule. If your patch falls off before 72 hours, apply a new patch to a different skin site and contact your doctor. Do NOT apply extra patches to make up for a missed one unless your doctor tells you to.
storage: Store unused patches at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep them in their original sealed pouches and away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Keep ALL patches — both new and used — completely out of reach of children and pets. Even a used patch contains enough medicine to seriously harm or kill a child. Used patches must be folded sticky-side together and flushed down the toilet immediately after removal.
what_to_avoid: - Do NOT drink alcohol while using this patch. It greatly increases the risk of dangerous breathing problems and can be life-threatening. This includes beer, wine, liquor, and any medicines or mouthwashes that contain alcohol. - Avoid sleeping pills, anti-anxiety medicines, muscle relaxers, or other opioid pain medicines unless your doctor approves, as combining them can cause dangerous or fatal breathing problems. - Avoid applying heat directly over the patch (heating pads, electric blankets, heat lamps, hot tubs, saunas, sunbathing). Heat makes the medicine absorb much faster, which can cause an overdose. - Do NOT drive, operate heavy machinery, or do dangerous activities until you know how this medicine affects you, as it can cause dizziness, drowsiness, and slowed reaction times. - Do NOT allow others to use your patch. Sharing this medicine is illegal and can cause death in someone who is not opioid-tolerant.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you or someone around you notices: - Slow, shallow, or stopped breathing - Extreme sleepiness, limpness, or difficulty waking up - Choking or gurgling sounds - Blue or purple color of the lips, fingertips, or skin - Confusion, extreme dizziness, or fainting - Chest pain or a very slow or irregular heartbeat - Signs of overdose: pinpoint (very small) pupils, cold or clammy skin, extreme weakness Also call your doctor if you experience: - Severe constipation - Nausea or vomiting that does not go away - Signs of serotonin syndrome: agitation, fast heartbeat, high fever, muscle twitching - Signs of adrenal problems: nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, unusual tiredness, weakness - Your pain is not well controlled or you feel you need more medicine - A skin rash or irritation where the patch is applied - You accidentally touch a used patch or if a child or pet is exposed to the patch
when_it_works: Fentanyl patches work slowly. It takes about 12 to 24 hours after you first apply the patch to reach a steady pain-relieving level in your blood. Your doctor may prescribe a short-acting pain medicine to help with pain during this first day. Once you are on a regular schedule and the right dose, the patch provides steady, around-the-clock pain relief. Do not expect the patch to work immediately like a pill would.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and over): Older adults may be more sensitive to fentanyl and have a higher risk of breathing problems, dizziness, and falls. Your doctor may start you on a lower dose and watch you more closely. Children: Fentanyl patches should NOT be used in children under 2 years of age, and are generally only used in children who are already tolerant to opioids. Keep patches completely away from all children — accidental exposure can be fatal. Pregnancy: Fentanyl can harm your unborn baby. Using this medicine during pregnancy, especially near the time of delivery, can cause serious breathing problems and withdrawal symptoms in the newborn. Tell your doctor immediately if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Fentanyl passes into breast milk and can seriously harm a nursing baby. Do not breastfeed while using this patch. Kidney or liver problems: If you have kidney or liver disease, your body may process this medicine more slowly, increasing the risk of side effects. Your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more carefully.
